meta.title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
meta.one_liner: A negotiation every week, a debrief every week, and a real negotiation of your own at the end.
meta.blurb: Every Monday students negotiated a role-play case against a classmate, and every Wednesday we took apart what happened: who claimed value, who created it, and what they left on the table. The cases built from a two-party price haggle to multi-party coalitions, mediation, social dilemmas, and a cross-cultural deal over a theme park. Alongside the cases, each student started the semester with a single KitKat and traded up as far as they could. The course ended with a paper on a real negotiation each student planned and carried out outside class.

assignments.name: Real world negotiation paper
assignments.description: Plan and carry out a negotiation outside class for anything you would actually be willing to buy or sell, then write it up in 2,000 words or fewer. The best papers built a scoring system for their own interests, estimated the other side's reservation price with honest uncertainty, and were self-critical about what they left on the table.

assignments.name: Post-negotiation journals
assignments.description: Three two-page journals over the semester, each sent to the instructor and to the other people in that negotiation. The point was reflection on what you were thinking, not a blow-by-blow account, and the counterpart's journal gave a rare view from the other side.

assignments.name: Pop quizzes
assignments.description: Five quizzes through the semester on the readings and concepts.

assignments.name: Attendance and class discussion
assignments.description: Every negotiation needs a prepared partner, so missing one without arranging a substitute cost a third of a letter grade.

assignments.name: Negotiation plans
assignments.description: A planning document handed in for each in-class negotiation: issues and their values, BATNA, reservation price, target, sources of power, and an opening move.

assignments.name: KitKat trade-up
assignments.description: Modeled on the One Red Paperclip story. Each student started with a KitKat and made at least three trades, logging every one, then wrote a one-page analysis of the tactics they used. On the last day the class voted on the best final item. It counted toward participation.
